newsitem.title: CONGO: South African icebreaker hosts Zaire talks.
newsitem.headline: South African icebreaker hosts Zaire talks.

text.p: After two days of uncertainty and sometimes undignified manoeuvring, Zaire's civil war rivals joined South Africa's Nelson Mandela on a customised icebreaker off Africa on Sunday to talk peace.

The Russian-built SAS Outeniqua -- an incongruity for a country little used to sea ice at home -- is a support vessel for South Africa's permanent Antarctic expedition but it occasionally has other missions.
For veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko, who is fighting cancer and a revolt at home, it was his second time on board the South African naval ship dubbed "The Grey Diplomat".
The ship was unable to dock at Gabon's capital Libreville, Mobutu's preferred embarcation point, because of its size.

With his doctors advising caution, Mobutu boarded the ship with great difficulty on Friday in Congo's port of Pointe Noire. Unable to climb 31 steep steps, he was driven on board five hours late up a makeshift ramp.
At one stage, the negotiators had envisaged hoisting him on by crane, sources close to the talks said.
Mobutu left the ship on Friday evening after sailing with Mandela into international waters for a rendezvous that Kabila failed to keep, citing security concerns.
Kabila, whose forces control three quarters of Zaire and are advancing towards the gates of the capital Kinshasa, boarded the ship by helicopter late on Saturday.
Mandela, who has staked his reputation on brokering a peaceful end to the war, was spending a third day on the ship.
Here are a few key facts about the ship:
* bought at a fire-sale price from Russia in 1993, it is the depleted South African Navy's newest, biggest and ugliest ship
* the slate-grey 21,025-tonne ship is 166-metre (545-foot) long
* Outeniqua takes its name from a mountain range inshore from South Africa's Indian Ocean port of Mossel Bay
* the South Africans nickname it "the Grey Diplomat"
* in 1993, it delivered a 130-bed portable field hospital to Trieste in Italy from South African to Bosnian Moslems
* it spent its commissioning cruise delivering medical supplies to Indian Ocean islands
* in 1995, it transported 2,000 former political prisoners to a reunion with Mandela on Robben Island off Cape Town
* initially called the Juvent, Russia built it in 1991 as a commercial ice-breaker with military specifications.
* it cost South Africa $12.8 million -- around a third of its replacement cost.
* it has two luxury suites on either side of the accommodation block awkwardly perched near the bow
* it boasts a well-equipped hospital
* the galley is able to serve the Zairean rivals and their host food as good as they will get anywhere.
* "For a naval vessel, she's really quite comfortable," Captain Fred Marais says
* a pad on the stern can handle most medium-sized helicopters
* it carries two Puma helicopters and is capable of a modest 17.5 knots.
* the mid-section is an almost clear space for cargo work or container transport
* with the supply ship Drakensberg it is the navy's only full-sized vessel. The rest are locally built patrol boats or Israeli gunboats.
